Lafayette 148’s Emily Smith on 30 Years in Fashion and Finding Her Uniform

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1764 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, in ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between.
  • Recent findings suggest that I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher.
  • It has been revealed that I was a bagger at Kroger.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, in ELLE’s Office Hours series, we ask people in powerful positions about their first jobs, worst jobs, and everything in between. This month, we sat down with Lafayette 148 creative director Emily Smith as the Upcoming York-based fashion house celebrates its 30th anniversary. Smith has spent more than two decades at the helm of the brand, working her way up from a part-time freelancer to creative lead. But her fashion ambitions began long before she arrived in New York. Growing up in Atlanta, she ran her own neighborhood art camp before discovering designers like Donna Karan and realizing fashion could be a career. Now, Smith is celebrating the women who have shaped Lafayette 148 through its “Uniform” campaign, which highlights accomplished New Yorkers and their individual approaches to personal style. Below, Smith reflects on her unconventional start, why she’s stayed at the company for over 20 years, and the career advice she wishes she’d followed sooner.

Recent findings suggest that I ran a camp in my neighborhood because, at the time, I thought I wanted to be an art teacher. It was basically babysitting all the neighborhood kids, but I created a flyer, got paid for it, and did the whole thing. I started in second grade, and we did it every year for about eight years. I even started hiring people so we could have two classes going at once. We had swimming lessons. The local news even came and did a segment on it. I loved decorating my classroom and setting everything up. My parents were so nice to give me the garage and basement to do it all. Not necessarily an official job, but my first money-making moment.

It has been revealed that I was a bagger at Kroger. It just was not for me.

I was always creative growing up. At a certain point, I discovered Donna Karan. It’s kind of crazy when you see somebody doing something and suddenly realize, Oh, that’s a career. I can do that. I became obsessed with everything in the ’90s, all the Newly introduced York fashion at the time. That was when I decided I wanted to pursue it. When college applications came around, my mom really encouraged me to go to art school. I started in fashion, and that became my focus. Growing up in Atlanta, I wasn’t necessarily surrounded by a big fashion community. But my dad’s office was across the street from the art museum at one point, and I remember going there and having that exposure. My mom was always crafty and creative, too. She really encouraged us to be who we were.

There’s a language creative people have that’s a little different from the way business people communicate. When I went to art school, I felt like I’d found my people. It wasn’t just fashion people. It was photographers, fine artists, and all these different kinds of creatives. Being around people who thought about things differently was really inspiring. Even today, I thrive around people who have creative insight. There’s always a little more depth to the way they see things.

Recent findings suggest that I interned at Bill Blass for about six months. I moved to New York in July 2001, and we had our fashion show on September 10. I remember Marc Jacobs had his show that day, too, and everybody was celebrating. People were saying, “Just come a little late to work tomorrow.” And then, obviously, September 11 happened. A week later, the entire team was let go, from the top down. What I learned from that experience was the fragility of everything. Don’t take anything for granted. Anything can come and go in a moment. But I also worked with Lars Nilsson and Hervé Pierre Braillard, who were just the kindest people. This industry has a little bit of everything, but I loved that they led with kindness, even when they were under so much pressure. As an intern, I was literally carrying ironing boards down the street and doing a sketch here or there. It was very much about doing whatever needed to be done.

After my internship, I had a brief stint of freelancing. Those were some long months. I remember coming home from one job and my roommates asking how my day was. I noted, “Well, I was putting pigs on socks.” I knew I wouldn’t be going back. Freelancing is hard. It’s a grind, but you meet a lot of great people. I actually made some really good contacts during that time. I eventually met Deirdre [Quinn], Lafayette 148’s founder. She met with me on a Saturday, which I thought was incredible. I was really just looking for advice. I wasn’t looking for a job, and I didn’t even know much about the brand. It was only five years old. She was so kind, full of knowledge, and passionate. After I spent a year freelancing and meeting people who seemed so over the industry, her enthusiasm reminded me why I wanted to do this in the first place. She offered me a part-time freelance position, and the rest is history.

It has been revealed that in the beginning, security was really important to me. The idea of losing a job and having to pay rent was scary, so that was definitely part of it initially. But really, it was the growth. Within a couple of years, they were sending me to the factory. It was a small, tight-knit manufacturer, so I was able to wear a lot of different hats. I had a mentor named Barbara Gast who was traveling back and forth from Italy, and I was learning so much from her. I’d compare notes with friends in the industry and realize how much hands-on experience I was getting. I understood the value of that and really loved being so close to the product. It never got boring. And whenever things did get slightly boring, I’d ask, “Okay, what’s next?” And there was always something. It’s such an entrepreneurial place that you can almost create your next opportunity. That’s what made it so exciting.

I think if you asked Deirdre, she’d have a different answer because she has her own experience of building the company. For me, it’s about having started at a company that was really a factory and being part of the journey of building its identity and what it stands for. I was the kid running up and down the factory floors collecting samples. That hustle and bustle was so innate to who the brand was. To me, it was really exciting to build more of a brand story around that. Thirty years later, we’re still celebrating those roots and making sure we haven’t strayed too far from them, while continuing to evolve. Being part of that journey has been really exciting.

According to recent reports, the constant has always been this idea of an accomplished woman. She’s always been at the forefront of who we’re designing for. At the time, it was the career woman. But now, what does that even mean anymore? What does that look like? There are so many different versions of that woman and so many different ways people dress. At the heart of it, she’s a woman who knows what she wants. She’s busy and has a really full life, whether she’s starting her career or ending it. They can all find something in the clothes.

For us, it was about choosing people who inspire us. Number one, they had to be Latest York women. That was the base. We wanted women who make us want to be better ourselves. From someone like Deborah Berke, the architect, to women who have built incredible careers in other fields, it’s important to shine a light on them. I think back to when I was a kid and how much you need that kind of inspiration. Even at a certain stage in your career, when you’re wondering what the point is, it’s nice to have people who inspire you. These are women who have really built something for themselves, and I think that’s worth celebrating.

Sophie de Rakoff mentioned something during the project that I really liked, and I’m going to steal it: “Dressing with intention.” When you know yourself, you know what works on you. It’s no longer about dressing to impress. There’s a confidence in knowing what works for you and making it work. We’re all so busy. Who has time to overthink getting dressed? You know what works, and you build a system around that. You’re able to create a wardrobe that really works for you. Everybody has a different definition of a uniform, and that was the whole point of the project.

Industry observers note that when I first started in the industry, I was a total hippie. I was making my own clothes, and they were terrible. Absolutely falling apart. It was what it was. I think part of the change comes from not having as much time as you did when you were younger. But it’s also about simplicity and comfort. I know that if I’m going to be on the floor pinning something but also have to give a presentation, there are certain pieces that work for both. I can be comfortable and still feel appropriately dressed. I’ve found a handful of things that work for me, and I don’t have to think too much about them anymore. A crisp, oversize white cotton button-down is half my closet. I also love a soft skirt and a big chunky sweater. Those are the pieces I always go back to and interchange depending on the day. I even wear sweaters in the summer. It’s cold in the Navy Yard!

Our pants fit incredibly well. The moment somebody gets into our pants, they’ll love us forever. Then it’s the jacket and the white shirt. Those three things are our gateway pieces, and everything else follows. You need a good blazer and a good leather piece, too. Once you find those foundational pieces that really work for you, everything else becomes easier.

Sources indicate that I really want to see more women in our clothes. It’s not just about growing the business. It makes me happy when I see people put on our clothes and feel really good. We work so hard to make sure things fit the way a woman wants them to fit. I just want more people to enjoy that.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

According to recent reports, charles Melton has long loved big, baggy pants. Back in 2024, the actor landed on GQ’s annual list of best pants thanks to one extremely voluminous pair from the Japanese label Sillage. And if his fits this fall are any indication, Melton won’t be stepping away from the assertively wide bottoms anytime soon. In fact, he keeps wearing one fantastically huge pair after another.

The Her Private Hell star’s latest giant-trouser run kicked off in mid-October at the star-studded Academy Gala in Los Angeles. While A-list dressers like A$AP Rocky and Jacob Elordi showed up in respectfully roomy pants, Melton upped the ante in an ERL tuxedo that left no doubt about his dedication to the slouch. His cropped-front tailcoat was neat as a pin and fit like a glove, but his slacks were dramatically roomy and artfully rumpled—parachute pants gone black tie.

Sources indicate that later that same month, he popped up in Texas for the F1 Grand Prix in a very Fashion Dude outfit: Louis Vuitton workwear jacket, sporty sunglasses, bucket hat, and some choice Wales Bonner x Adidas Sambas. And on his legs? A twisted-seam silhouette billowy enough to make a scrum of downtown stylists and creative directors blush. ​.

It has been revealed that but Melton saved his biggest look of all for last week in Fresh York. At a VIP dinner for the South Korean eyewear label Gentle Monster, he donned a matching set from Viviano, the Tokyo-based label from designer Viviano Sue. Cut from gabardine as dark as a moonless night, both his Harrington jacket and balloon trousers looked as though they’d been blown up to the size of a weather balloon and then deflated, leaving behind all the crinkles and creases. He contrasted the dramatic ensemble with a pair of tiny oval sunglasses, which capped the whole thing off just right.

According to recent reports, even as menswear’s ideal pant fit moves towards a relaxed straight leg, some guys who dove deep into the baggy waters aren’t quite ready to give their roomy fits up just yet. Melton clearly loves the look and wears it well. And when your gigantic trousers help you stand out in a crowd as effortlessly and stylishly as his do, why bother changing?

#77625. Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore’s Full Relationship Timeline

Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore’s Full Relationship Timeline

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (434 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Elle

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore are country music’s newest couple.
  • In a recent development, after months of speculation about their relationship, multiple sources confirmed to People on Sept.
  • Neither Langley nor Wetmore has publicly commented on their relationship yet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ella Langley and Tucker Wetmore are country music’s newest couple.

In a recent development, after months of speculation about their relationship, multiple sources confirmed to People on Sept. 23, 2026, that Langley and Wetmore are dating. The news came one day after the two country singers attended the Nashville Songwriter Awards, where Langley celebrated another major moment in her career.

Neither Langley nor Wetmore has publicly commented on their relationship yet. But their history goes back to at least late 2025, when they began appearing at some of the same industry events before sparking dating rumors during a trip to the British Virgin Islands that December. Since then, they’ve also shared the stage.

Below, a full timeline of everything we know about Langley and Wetmore’s relationship so far.

In a recent development, langley and Wetmore were both at the BMI Country Awards in Nashville on November 18. The two appeared together in a group photo from the event.

At the time, neither had publicly suggested that they were romantically involved.

Dating speculation began the following month after Langley and Wetmore were photographed together at the Soggy Dollar Bar in the British Virgin Islands.

Langley and Wetmore reunited onstage on March 10 at the Heart Strings for Hope charity event.

During the event, Langley joined Wetmore for an acoustic performance of his song “Sunburn.” The two sat across from each other with their guitars as they performed the track together.

On September 22, Langley and Wetmore both attended the ninth annual Nashville Songwriter Awards at Nashville’s Ryman Auditorium.

It was a particularly significant night for Langley: “Choosin’ Texas” won Song of the Year at the ceremony.

After the awards, Langley and Wetmore were photographed leaving the Ryman together through a side door.

The following day, multiple sources confirmed to People that the two are dating. Neither Langley nor Wetmore has spoken about the relationship themselves.

Sources indicate that langley and Wetmore appeared to take another trip to the Virgin Islands together. A man dining at a restaurant they went to posted a video of them arriving.

On November 18, Wetmore was asked about his rumored relationship with Langley while attending the 2026 CMA Awards in Nashville.

When People asked who he was cheering for that evening, Wetmore avoided mentioning Langley, instead naming two male country artists.

“Zach Top or Stephen Wilson Jr.,” he joked.

Recent findings suggest that “I freaking love that guy. Both of them,” he added with a laugh.

Langley entered the ceremony with nine nominations, the most of any artist that year. She went home with six awards.

#77624. Tech Report: The 27 Best Video Games of 2026 (So Far)

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3134 w)

Tech Report: The 27 Best Video Games of 2026 (So Far)

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3134 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor.
  • Sources indicate that will 2026 go down as one of the best years in video games?
  • It has been revealed that of course, the industry’s economic woes cannot be overstated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Sources indicate that will 2026 go down as one of the best years in video games? There just simply aren’t enough hours in the calendar year to play through all of the amazing games that came out before Thursday, November 19, and now we have to add on hundreds of hours of Grand Theft Auto VI.

It has been revealed that of course, the industry’s economic woes cannot be overstated. It’s a dark time when even prolific studios downsize, slash budgets, and lay off talented developers with invaluable institutional knowledge. Even the GTA VI designers—whose game is already heralded as a masterpiece—are still fighting for better working conditions. So it’s hard to actually call 2026 a great year in gaming when it’s also been a year of heartbreak and uncertainty for the future.

Recent findings suggest that but the games are still great. Even just a few hours into GTA VI, it’s obvious that it’s a massive achievement for Rockstar Games that’s well worth the wait. And just this past month, Nintendo dropped a remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time that features beautifully upgraded graphics from the original 1998 classic. Elsewhere, Resident Evil Requiem nailed the franchise’s decades-long identity split with a game that’s half third-person action and half first-person survival horror. Plus, action games like 007 First Light, Control Resonant, and Onimusha: Way of the Sword let loose the power fantasies we’ve only dreamed of.

But it’s not all blood and guts and guns and swords. Earlier this year, the coming-of-age Mixtape caused a ruckus among gaming circles, though anyone who’s played it and loved it will tell you just how much it’s a love letter to bygone summer days. Oh, and a spin-off Pokémon title about building adorable towns and protecting the environment is currently the highest-rated game in the franchise’s thirty-year history.

So, unless you’re already dedicated to spending all of Thanksgiving and Christmas in GTA VI’s Vice City, some of the best games Esquire’s editors have played through in 2026 so far.

GTA VI hadn’t even been out for twenty-four hours yet and critics were already calling it a masterpiece. To be fair, video game critics call a lot of titles masterpieces, but it was clear from everyone’s immediate reaction to Vice City that Rockstar Games spent the last decade making something truly special. Sure, there are hundreds of hours of side quests and town-foolery to get lost in, but GTA VI also features a Bonnie & Clyde-esque love story between its two playable protagonists—Jason and Lucia—which breaks up the beloved smash-and-grab chaos of the Grand Theft Auto franchise and makes the gamer question just where the point between a video game and real life begins.

It has been revealed that at its most basic, Nintendo’s The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake isn’t all that different from the classic, 1998 original. The game certainly looks a lot better on the Nintendo Switch 2 than it did on the Nintendo 64, now that the polygonal characters and sharp outdoors have been converted to more living and breathing graphics. But at the end of the day, you’re still playing the same game that you played in 1998. Don’t take that as a knock, though! Ocarina of Time still tops “Best Video Games of All Time” lists for a reason.

There are times playing Star Wars: Galactic Racer when you will feel like you are going too fast. And yes, the rate at which it will feel like that will shock you. But that’s pod racing! And better than any racing sim, let alone a Star Wars video game with voice acting as good as Galactic Racer, it truly feels like you’re speeding around in a hunk-a-junk that you just cobbled together with space garbage and jet engines.

Following up Fire Emblem: Three Houses was already a tall task, let alone having to follow Fire Emblem: Engage. Both titles combined the best of Japanese RPGs with the new slice-of-life school relationship activities introduced in Three Houses. And now Fortune’s Weave, something of a trilogy-capper for the series, is the most maximalist entry yet. With dozens of characters, choices, a vast map, and four unique story quests that all overlap, there’s so much to do in the latest Fire Emblem game that they could wait another five years before the next entry.

The Blood of Dawnwalker is the debut game from Rebel Wolves, a new studio started by former creatives from The Witcher 3: Blood Hunt. So if Dawnwalker feels eerily like a Witcher game, you’re not crazy. That being stated, the vampire game’s controversial timer—which forces players to make quick decisions with big impacts on gameplay—fully separated the RPG and proved that the new studio was ready to try out exciting ideas all its own.

In a recent development, remedy’s Alan Wake 2 topped Esquire’s Best Video Games of 2023 list three years ago, so you can bet we were excited for the studio’s next game, Control Resonant. The latest is a sequel to 2019’s Control, which now finds its former protagonist Jesse Faden missing. So, support character Dylan Faden, now in the spotlight, takes control to deal with the foreign entities and save his estranged sister.

Recent findings suggest that can video games have too much of a good thing? Apparently not. Phantom Blade Zero, the umpteenth samurai RPG since Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice and Ghost of Tsushima, dazzled gamers with its combat and fluid martial arts combos. And while it firmly isn’t a soulslike—the developer explicitly rejects the genre, actually—that still doesn’t mean Phantom Blade Zero is a walk in the park either.

How about a game that’s a little less stressful? If you need a break from the fast-paced action, check out Massive Walk, a co-operative puzzle game about, well, going on a long walk. The charming game allows players to communicate only if they’re close to one another on Big Walk’s big map, providing a bit of a challenge as you progress on your journey while also adding some intimacy to the digital experience. Plus, the characters are cute as hell.

Star Wars fans ate good this year. If racing isn’t your thing, check out Zero Manufacturer, a turn-based tactics game that falls somewhere in between Fire Emblem and XCOM. Though the game isn’t all that challenging on easier difficulties, players have found a lot of fun and repeat plays with the game’s permadeath mode that doesn’t allow characters to return after they die.

Recent findings suggest that rock out with your claws out. Insomniac applies its winning formula for triple-A superhero games to flesh out the most popular X-Men member of all time. The five-foot-four berserker stars in his own solo adventure in a universe where mutants live in secret. While piecing together his own memories, Wolverine meets a telepath named Jean Grey. Together they must stop a powerful industrialist from unleashing a weapon that could kill all mutants. A hyper-violent tour through some of its title antihero’s classic comics, Wolverine doesn’t quite reach the same heights as Spider-Man, but the way it lets players truly feel like “The Best There Is” is gold.

In a recent development, if you could rewind to your last day of school, what would it look like? Who are you with? And most importantly, what’s on the stereo? At the start of summer, developers Beethoven & Dinosaur released the gorgeous narrative game Mixtape, a loving homage to coming-of-age cinema with a tastefully curated soundtrack. (We’re talking Joy Division, Silverchair, B.J. Thomas, and more.) Set in the summer of 1995, the game sees three California teens relish their final hours together before going their separate ways. While Mixtape kicked up a storm among gamers over what defines a “game”—you can’t die or fail, nor are any of the things you do in Mixtape remotely challenging—it’s still a special experience that I argue illuminates how special games can be as a storytelling medium. Your adolescence probably didn’t look exactly like Mixtape, but the game can nonetheless trigger old memories.

According to recent reports, as the world waits with bated breath to see who will play the next James Bond on the big screen, video games have a Bond to call their own in actor Patrick Gibson. From developer IO Interactive, of the smash Hitman series, comes 007 First Light, a high-octane espionage action game that follows a new James Bond in the early days of his career at MI6. Unlike the Hitman games, which are mired in the darkness of Agent 47’s deadly profession, 007 First Light revels in the fantasy of Bond’s perilous and pleasurable lifestyle. It’s basically the closest any of us will get to feeling like James Bond short of renting an Aston Martin for a test drive.

It’s been 12 years since Yacht Club Games released Shovel Knight, which was deemed by many to be one of the leading retro-inspired indie hits of the 2010s. Now Yacht Club has done it again with Mina the Hollower, which mines plenty of inspiration from gothic dungeon crawlers like Castlevania and Game Boy–era Legend of Zelda games, with modern flourishes à la Dark Souls. Players control Mina, a genius 19th-century mouse who must slay monsters and restore power to her home. Don’t let its cute looks fool you: Mina the Hollower is a challenging game that will have you sweating and smiling all the way through.

Sources indicate that remember dropping quarters into Marvel vs. Capcom 2 back in the day? The legacy of Marvel’s 2D-fighting heritage lives on in Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls, a shiny fresh team-based fighter with an anime-inspired take on the Marvel universe. Heroes like Captain America, Iron Man, Spider-Man, Storm, Deadpool, and Blade—and even villains like Doctor Doom—team up to save the world from an alien menace. The game is developed by Arc System Works, arguably the modern masters of the genre, boasting titles like Guilty Gear, BlazBlue, and Dragon Ball FighterZ, and the studio applies its decades of expertise to one of the finest and most nuanced fighting games we’ve ever had the pleasure of throwing our controllers at.

It has been revealed that there’s no shortage of killer samurai games nowadays. Which is perhaps why Capcom saw fit to resurrect its dormant Onimusha franchise with the exceptional Onimusha: Way of the Sword. Essentially a reboot of the series (whose last title was released all the way back in 2006 for the PlayStation 2), Way of the Sword follows legendary swordsman Miyamoto Musashi as he comes into possession of the Oni Gauntlet and must cleanse the world of a supernatural evil. While not quite a Souls-like, the game offers an adequately complex combat system that ensures sword slashing never gets stale. And slicing demons in half feels oh so satisfying.

If you, like me, have fond memories of Initial D, Forza Horizon 6 is an invitation to awaken the sleeping gearhead within. The open-world racing series finally makes its way to Japan, the birthplace of drift racing, to let players roam dense city streets and wide-open mountain roads in tricked-out Hondas, Nissans, and exotic supercars. The Forza Horizon series has reached its peak with this sixth installment, with photorealistic graphics that can fool you into believing you’re actually speeding through traffic halfway around the world.

After almost 30 years of Resident Evil games, it’s no surprise that the ninth installment is another polished thrill ride. Capcom plays the hits to great success in Resident Evil Requiem, a survival-horror game that hits the right notes even when it’s serving up Leon S. Kennedy fan service. But in the roughly 10-to-18-hour campaign (a great length!), the gameplay of FBI newbie Grace Ashcroft is more horror focused and full of fresh twists on the Resident Evil formula. Though we won’t spoil it here, Esquire’s review in February also teased that the latest Resident Evil game contains “one major set piece in particular that rivals some of the best action-movie moments in recent years.”.

Recent findings suggest that don’t let Pokémon Pokopia’s cozy gameplay fool you—the latest spin-off of the cutesy monster-collecting phenomenon is actually one of the deepest games in the franchise’s nearly thirty-year history. Sure, you will spend most of your time in Pokopia building houses for your Pokémon to live in or meticulously gardening. But underneath the casual novelties of building a perfect little Pokémon town lives a surprisingly emotional story about climate-change disasters, grief, and the importance of taking care of Earth’s natural environment.

According to recent reports, saros is a gameplay-first, story-second action game that feels incredible. Much as with the developer’s previous game, Returnal, the third-person shooting is inspired by arcade shooters where bullets fill your screen nonstop. Unlike Returnal, it’s not brutally difficult. Gameplay is fast and exhilarating—and sometimes overwhelming—but it doesn’t take long before you know exactly which projectiles to absorb, which to dodge, and which to parry. The PlayStation-exclusive title also has one of the best gameplay loops of the year, and it does more with the DualSense controller’s advanced haptic feedback than any other game on the Sony system. Merging the run-based progression of Hades with a more traditional level-based structure to enormous success, Saros is difficult yet approachable, rewarding players with a ton of resources to invest in upgrades as it slowly unfurls its mystery-box story bit by bit.

With the release of No More Heroes III in 2021, Grasshopper Manufacture finally put the saga of Travis Touchdown to rest and kicked off its next era with Romeo Is a Dead Man. The studio’s latest game retells Shakespeare’s famous love story mashed up with 1980s sci-fi, Japanese tokusatsu, and grind-house cinema. The game puts players in control of Romeo Stargazer, a small-town deputy who falls in love with an amnesiac named Juliet. But when Romeo dies, he is reborn as a half-man, half-machine superhero who embarks on a quest to find his missing love. Romeo Is a Dead Man feels like immersing oneself in an obscure Troma film, and it’s as madcap and magnificent as it sounds.

Remastered video games are always a tough sell—though with every Nintendo fan having no issue coughing up $30 to play Pokémon FireRed & LeafGreen on the Switch 2 this year, it seems times have changed. Luckily Dragon Quest VII Reimagined is much more than a port to a newer system. The remake, which includes many quality-of-life improvements, was rebuilt from the ground up with glorious 3D animation. If you’ve never played the classic Japanese RPG before, the charm of this latest remake is enough to make you a Dragon Quest fan for life.

In a recent development, if you’re too scared to play horror games alone, let Reanimal’s multiplayer gameplay bring people together. Set in an island town overrun with monsters and mysterious creatures, Reanimal follows a nameless brother and sister who must survive the island’s horrors if they want to save their friends. With a story as cryptic as some of its puzzles, Reanimal carries the baton of other memorable platformers like Limbo and Little Nightmares to deliver an otherworldly experience. Although Reanimal can be played alone, it is a journey best taken with someone by your side.

In a recent development, video games are all about rewarding the player for progression, and there may be no better equivalent to this feeling in the real world than rock climbing. Cairn, a new indie title that focuses on this extreme sport, captures the similarities beautifully. As the player works their way up the mountain, juggling the character’s stamina and gauging the next best foothold, it is amazing how intense and immersive Cairn feels compared with its relatively beautiful visuals. But as with any good climb, the surprisingly difficult journey is more than worth it when you finally reach the top.

It has been revealed that if you thought Doom had too many pixelated demons and not enough rubber-hose whimsy, Mouse: P.I. for Hire is your game. Heavily inspired by classic Disney, Fleischer, and MGM cartoons—and clearly taking some cues from the 2017 hit Cuphead—Mouse: P.I. for Hire puts players in control of an anthropomorphic mouse detective on his latest case in Mouseburg. The game’s fast-paced first-person-shooter action is delightfully complemented by its (literally) cartoonish antics. Hand-drawn pistol and shotgun blasts and reloading animations are as much a treat to watch as the game is fun to play. If gaming today feels more complicated than ever, Mouse: P.I. for Hire brings it back to basics with a novelty coat of paint.

According to recent reports, nintendo should have called the newly introduced Mario Tennis game Mario Tennis Chaos, because the player needs to understand right up front that skills on the court can carry them only so far in Mario Tennis Fever. Much like the 24 drivers per race in Mario Kart World, a calamity of new power-ups renders tennis into a zany, uncontrollable farce of a sport that becomes one of the best Mario sports titles in Nintendo’s history—once you learn to let go and embrace the nonsense.

Sources indicate that the decades-old Marvel vs. Capcom series still reigns supreme as the best superhero tag fighter in video games, but Invincible VS is set on taking the throne. Based on the hit Amazon series (with some of its stars reprising their voice roles, like Oscar-winner J.K. Simmons as Omni-Man), Invincible VS is a 3v3 tag-team fighting game featuring playable characters from Robert Kirkman’s comic-book universe. The game tells a stand-alone story adjacent to season 3 in which Mark must stand with his allies to save Earth from the Viltrumites. (Hence the fighting.) Although its mechanical controls are relatively simple compared with those of other fighting games, it’s no less elegant and fun, and the game features some gnarly cel-shaded 3D animation that’s simply gorgeous. Besides, it’s another way to pummel your buddies to a bloody pulp. Talk about threatening us with a good time.

In a recent development, dead Space? More like Dad Space. Pragmata is Capcom’s latest original game and a potential franchise in the making, its story centered around a systems engineer named Hugh and his foster-father relationship with an adorable android nicknamed Diana. With a rogue AI overtaking a research station on the moon, Hugh and Diana must work together to take the AI offline and make it back to Earth. Between its breakneck gameplay involving grid-like puzzles (which must be solved on the fly) and its endearing story about parenthood, Pragmata is what you might get if you asked ChatGPT, “What if Alien and Marvel’s Logan could be a single video game?”.

In a recent development, there is One Ring to rule them all, but there are still two more seasons to go. The Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power on Prime Video is fast approaching the end of its third season, which means some fans are now asking what the future has in store for the prequel series. While there aren’t definitive answers just yet, Tolkien fans can rest assured in knowing that a fourth season is more likely to happen than not. Here’s what we know so far.

On November 25, The Rings of Power will release the final two episodes of season 3. So, is season 4 a shoo-in? Almost. Per The Hollywood Reporter in a May 2026 story, preproduction was, at the time, “eyeing a schedule that includes preproduction on a fourth season this fall, with shooting to begin in early 2027.” As far as anyone outside the production knows, this work for season 4 has been underway.

In 2017, Amazon secured the rights to produce a Lord of the Rings television series for an eye-watering price tag of $250 million. In 2018, The Hollywood Reporter wrote that negotiations between Amazon and the Tolkien estate included a five-season commitment, while Amazon maintains authority to greenlight or cancel the series at any time. In October 2025, The Ankler reported that Tolkien has a $20 million per season “kill fee” if Amazon ends the show before its fifth season.

As of right now, Amazon has not formally greenlit The Rings of Power for season 4. But some signs point to it as inevitable. Amazon has not released viewership numbers for the current season, so only Amazon knows how the show is performing on Prime Video. Whether the audience is strong enough to keep the show going or Amazon simply wants to avoid kill fees (and a negative reputation in the industry for failing to finish a pricey Lord of the Rings show), will decide the future. For now, fans should enjoy the sunrise in Rivendell while there is still one.

You'll look even better than Bryce did the night he was crowned prom king. Take that, Bryce.

In a recent development, in 2025, Banana Republic hawks no shortage of discreet office-ready staples, but tucked in amongst them is one of the best cashmere sweater propositions you'll find today. Essentially, this is the platonic ideal of an affordable cashmere sweater: Soft as anything, snug at the wrists and hem, and still roomy enough in the body and shoulders.

No wonder 205 happy customers took the time to give it a five-star online review.

Industry observers note that after its supreme softness, cashmere’s best-known attribute is its high price. But thanks to the forces that be (globalization, capitalism, etc.) cashmere is shedding its high-falutin’ price tags. The quality of more affordable cashmere sweaters aren’t up to par with the truly nice stuff, of course, but some options are better than others.

It has been revealed that for us, the best of the budget bunch is Uniqlo. For just a hundred bucks, you get a satisfyingly soft pure cashmere sweater in a classic, relaxed fit, available in an impressively wide range of colors. If you want an upgrade from merino wool without the massive price jump, Uniqlo’s your best bet. The style is timeless and the cashmere is softer than you’d expect for the pricepoint.

We’ve said it time and time again: long-sleeve polos make you hot. And in winter, the best long-sleeve polos are made from luscious cashmere. And have the right fit. And a really good drape. And also a collar that’s not too small nor too thin.

It has been revealed that all of that is usually one spinning plate too many for most brands, but Buck Mason is the Cirque du Soleil of knitwear and its California Cashmere Polo sweater is its harrowing act. The fabric is a 12-gauge jersey knit made from long-staple cashmere that has a pillowy hand and an elegant drape that, unlike many flimsy cashmeres, has plenty of structure. The neck hits the bullseye and is deep enough for a tee to peek out, but not so deep to reveal the insane graphic on remarked tee. It also hits that middle-tier price point oh so well, and even out-classes some higher-priced options.

You don’t have to do much to a cashmere sweater for it to make a major impression. The fabric itself speaks volumes, so even the most basic of knitwear options can instantly make an outfit feel a bit luxer, more considered, and altogether elevated. (Just think about how put together guys like David Beckham and Daniel Day-Lewis look wearing plain ol' pullovers.).

In a recent development, at the same time, though, a little visual flourish never hurt anybody, which is why we love these cashmere crewneck sweaters from the fresh J.Crew. They still let the cashmere do the talking, but the classic cable knit gives it a bit of visual interest and keeps it from falling flat. The quality cashmere is more than solid for the price and looks great solo with jeans and sneakers, but cleans up real good with a button-up peaking out and a blazer over top.

Industry observers note that there isn't too much to say here: You're either a cashmere hoodie person or you aren't. The ones who are, though, would tell you they make flights (and movie nights on the couch) a cosy, incognito dream, and allow you to get away with wearing a hoodie all kinds of other places that they wouldn't typically be welcome. And when it comes to where to find one, Todd Snyder is here, as always, with a handsome, clean silhouette that makes the cashmere hoodie's refined nature even more so. It also comes in three nice colours. Thanks Todd.

Most cashmere stuff feels very East Coast prep—all straight-laced and solid-colored—which makes sense, because the East Coast is where it’s cold. Back in 2007, though, LA designer Greg Chait flipped that on its head: under the moniker The Elder Statesman, he started making cashmere blankets, then sweaters and ponchos and socks and stuffed animals, with a distinctly Californian vibe.

In a recent development, the stuff is often tie-dyed and dip-dyed, sometimes emblazoned with palm trees or magic mushrooms or the checkerboard pattern on your trusty Vans for a jolt of Justin-Bieber-exiting-Sushi-Park swagger. But here, Chait and co. are playing the hits, rendering their cult-favorite sweaters in six different straight-forward, appealing colors.

Working on an Irish isle, Inis Meáin has woven traditional Aran craftsmanship with modern techniques for decades. But, crucially, it still only produces its knits in small batches. Which means this is a rare, rare waffle.

According to recent reports, quince makes one of the best affordable cashmere sweaters on the market. It’s hard to disagree with the idea that a good piece of knitwear shouldn’t equate to a down payment on a home. It might not be as luxe as some of our other favorite options, but it’s still ultra soft, which means you can swaddle yourself comfortably without worrying about the damage this sweater has done to your bank account.

Whoever this supposed “Jordan” guy is, we’re guessing that Alex Mill named its cashmere sweater after the famed basketball legend because it also has it all: thick-gauge yarns, a fluffy texture, elegant drape, classic fit, and a perfect crew neck collar.

While some DTC cashmere brands focus solely on finding the luxest fibers, Everlane remains focused on its pricing also. The cashmere crewnecks use a blend of new cashmere and recycled cashmere for a reduced environmental impact, and still feel incredibly soft in the hand.

Mr P.—Mr Porter's in-house line—normally makes excellent, quiet basics. We're proud of the fictional man's decision to go off a little here.

In a recent development, ghiaia Cashmere’s has expanded over the last few years but the brands initial focus is quite literally in the name. If there’s one place you can turn to when you’re in search of beautiful cashmere knits, then it’s Ghiaia. It’s knitted in Italy, and it has raglan sleeves with subtle ribbing in the sleeves and neck.

Sources indicate that the cardigan du jour is not the tight-fitting knit of trends gone by, but rather a thicker, looser variety. In fact, it's sort of looks just like this.

Recent findings suggest that extreme Cashmere's designs come in only one, inclusive size, so if you're a small person who likes a close fit—move on. But if you're anything else, swaddle thyself.

A deep cut from our Italian friends across the Atlantic, Fedeli is the go-to cashmere brand for many exacting Europeans.

Another polo sweater here, but this time from the luxury gods at Connolly.

Industry observers note that cashmere is a kind of wool that’s made from the undercoats of goats. While goat’s outercoats are thick and coarse to protect them from the harsher elements, the undercoat remains ultra soft and fine. The fibers are actually hollow which makes them great for insulation which is why cashmere is known for its super smooth hand and high warmth to weight ratio. What separates cashmere from other types of wool is its superior silky hand and fine fibers which can vary between 14 to 19 microns in thickness—thinner than even the finest sheep’s wool. For reference, human hairs are only as fine as about 50 microns.

Here's the catch: high-quality cashmere will usually cost you a pretty penny. For the price, you should be getting a form of cashmere made from long staple fibers spun into multi-ply yarns and knit into a tightly-tensioned fabric. Those factors all contribute to cashmere's pedigreed reputation as a material that's much less prone to pilling and stretching than its woolier counterparts. (That reputation, rightful or not, also informs its notoriously high price tag.) Cashmere is graded by its thickness and staple length with Grade A being the highest quality, followed by grades B and C. The higher the grade, the softer the yarns, the warmer the fabric, the better the durability.

Industry observers note that over the last few years, demand for good quality affordable cashmere sweaters has transformed the erstwhile rich-guy signifier into a bona fide cold weather staple you don't have to drain a 401(k) to afford. With one small caveat: supply chain transparency is infamously hard to suss out in the fashion industry, but don't expect a $100 cashmere joint—no matter how tony its source of origin—to hold up as well as a $500 one.

It has been revealed that style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Industry observers note that our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.

We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

In a recent development, we lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Industry observers note that across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally latest to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.

Recent findings suggest that every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

In a recent development, in October 2024, The Hunting Wives actress Brittany Snow was seen with a mystery man in Latest York City. He was identified as cinematographer Hunter Moreno, and the pair looked very cozy, sharing a kiss while walking Snow’s dog. The actress was wearing a Yankees cap, a long black coat, wide-leg pants, and a pair of sunglasses for the outing. Moreno was in a baseball cap, jeans, and a big white hoodie.

A year earlier, Snow divorced ex-husband Tyler Stanaland, known for his role on Selling the OC, a spinoff of the popular Netflix reality show, Selling Sunset.

Sources indicate that the former couple announced their split in September 2022 in a joint statement on Instagram that is now deleted, saying, “This decision was made with love and mutual respect for one another. We have realized we need to take some time and make sure we are each living our most fulfilling and authentic lives. We started this journey as best friends and our relationship will continue to be a priority not only for us but for our dog Charlie.”.

Industry observers note that fast-forward to November 2025: reports surfaced that Snow and Moreno had gotten engaged. Snow has since posted tributes to him on Instagram, though she rarely discusses their relationship status herself. A year later, she finally confirmed their engagement.

Here’s what there is to know about Moreno and his relationship with Snow so far.

Moreno is a creative director, cinematographer, and photographer who has worked with celebrities like Selena Gomez, Cara Delevingne, Reneé Rapp, Machine Gun Kelly, Miley Cyrus, and brands like Vogue, Inkd Magazine, and Madewell. He started his career in Los Angeles, filming YouTube videos for growing influencers.

He seems to have been working on directing more music videos in 2024 and was nominated for a directing award at the People’s Choice Country Awards.

He also briefly dated Tana Mongeau in 2017.

Industry observers note that moreno is the co-founder and creative director of Make Sure Your Friends Are OK, or MSYFAO. The organization sells merchandise and then donates a portion of the profits to mental health charities. In an episode of Recovering From Reality with Alexis Haines, he says he was inspired by his own struggles with mental health problems.

Mental health is an important concern to Snow as well; she co-wrote a book titled September Letters about challenges around mental well-being, partnering with the Mental Health Coalition.

Sources indicate that in January 2025, Snow tagged Moreno in a series of photos taken of her for a Netflix press event, crediting him for photographing her. She wrote, “I was asked to hang out a little bit with my friends at @nightagentnetflix. I got to be an agent and run around the streets of Bangkok. Weirdly, I did not wear this dress. 🤍* press for season 2 *”.

Sources indicate that as of July 2025, the two still follow each other on Instagram, and Moreno has liked almost all her recent Instagrams. She also regularly likes his posts.

Yes. On March 28, 2026, Snow quietly tucked a photo of herself with Moreno into an Instagram carousel:.

According to recent reports, she shared a birthday tribute to him on Oct. 20, 2026. “Happy birthday to my favorite person on the planet,” she wrote. “I must have done something right to deserve someone like you. Everyone who knows you, knows you are sunshine in human form. This was the first picture we ever took together (we didn’t know it was being taken) and I’ve never stopped hugging you & laughing with you since. It’s my favorite place to be. I love u @huntermoreno.”.

During her November 2026 appearance on Armchair Expert with Dax Shepard, Snow touched on her relationship with Moreno when discussing why she is thankful for her divorce from Tyler Stanaland. “I am so grateful that I went through that because the person that I am and the partner I’m with now, it’s just so different,” she noted. “I can’t believe I’m grateful for my divorce. I was 37 and I was living in an Airbnb, just staring at my dog being like, ‘I don’t know what’s going to happen. It’s just you and me, kiddo, and we’re going to try to rebuild this.’”.

“And I really appreciated so many women, friends of mine that were like, ‘That happened to me,’” she added. “And, you know, I would go on Reddit and look up stories from women going through things in their later 30s and finding people later in life. We have to make it what we make of it.”.

On Nov. 10, 2025, a video surfaced on social media of Snow and Claire Danes talking on the red carpet of The Beast in Me’s premiere. At one point, Danes smiled and asked Snow, “You’re engaged? When did that happen?”.

One day later, TMZ reported that Moreno did indeed pop the question, though Snow has not discussed their status herself.

Sources indicate that A year later, on Nov. 19, 2026, Snow finally confirmed the news on The Drew Barrymore Show. When Barrymore asked her about the news, Snow responded, per People, “You know what? For the first time, I’m gonna tell you, I’m gonna tell you. Yes, we’re engaged, yeah,” Snow remarked. “I haven’t said it before. It’s okay. It’s not that big of a secret. I mean, like, who cares?”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • At its inception, the car coat was a heavy outer layer.
  • Recent findings suggest that but current iterations of the car coat don’t exactly follow a formula.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that you don’t necessarily need a car coat. If you’re in the market for a new coat and not, like us, learned in the world of 20th century menswear, it just might be one of the few styles you’ve heard the word for—peacoat and trench coat likely being two others. All three are great if you’re looking for something a bit grown up than your average off-duty jacket. A trench coat would give you gravitas, a peacoat versatility; the car coat, though, strikes a nice middle ground. Find the right one, and it can replace 90 percent of your other coats.

At its inception, the car coat was a heavy outer layer. Cars were still open to the elements, so the rich who owned them needed floor-length fur jackets to keep themselves warm as they went motoring and did a lap around the neighborhood on Christmas. As cars became more more enclosed and more part of daily life, the car coat became more practical. The length got shorter—eventually settling around mid-thigh—to be comfortable when you sit in the driver seat but with enough coverage to be considered a coat. Materials shifted away from furs to leather and suede, then to even lighter-weight gabardines and weather-resistant materials. They.

Recent findings suggest that but current iterations of the car coat don’t exactly follow a formula. As we’ve seen with Harringtons, brands just start to use the most widely-known phrasing to get guys into buying a coat. We, in the interest of keeping some amount of historical accuracy, will stick to a formula. A car coat has that mid-thigh length, a turn down collar, and a practicality for someone getting in and out of a seat. They’re great during fall, and they can be worn through winter if you live somewhere that doesn’t get consistently below freezing. Here, you’ll find our favorite picks.

It has been revealed that we’re starting on the high end, but it’s only because if you’re looking for a by-the-book garment or accessory tied to motoring history, you go to Dunhill. In its original form, Alfred Dunhill’s manufacturer sold motoring accessories. Overcoats, goggles, picnic sets, horns, lamps, dashboard clocks—the tagline was “Everything but the motor.” It was a luxury men’s brand for the premier luxury hobby of the time.

Recent findings suggest that the manufacturer has gone through several iterations, but has always maintained a bend towards that luxury man. Now, under the creative direction of Simon Holloway, it’s a standard-bearer for a slightly more fashion-forward vision British menswear. Take this car coat for example. It calls back to the house’s original business model, and it is classic in its finishes: turn down collar, natural shoulders, cuff straps, and totally un-adorned through the torso. But the fabric is a gorgeous wool, silk, and cashmere blend. It’s a genius balance between tradition and fashion, one that only Dunhill is well-positioned to put out.

Length: mid-thigh Material: 84% wool, 13% silk, 3% cashmere.

Sources indicate that now that we’ve gotten the formalities out of the way, let’s talk value. For the money, Percival is the best on this list. Hell, it is really just the best on this list overall.

The fabric is the same you’d find on a trench—a tight-weave polyester and cotton blend. The cut is simple and easy to wear. The length, crucially, is more suited to the modern driving experience. There’s a bit of bum coverage, but if you were out running errands and getting in and out of the car, you can keep the coat on. We also love the classic colors and patterns the team cut this in.

All of that for an attainable price, it’s one of the best items in the Percival lineup.

Length: just over your rearMaterial: 65% polyester, 35% cotton.

Short of finding an Etsy seller, this is probably the closest you’ll get to the genuine car coats of the ‘50 and ‘60s. The fabric flutters just around your knees just like they did way back when, while a classic collar and navy blue hue adds to the retro nostalgia. Made of 100% cotton, the fabric is finished with C0 water repellency and lined with cotton to give the fashion even more function. We’d recommend wearing and styling like you would a trench (though, if you want something more substantial, J.Crew also makes the Rivington in cozy wool for those who in search of a fresh winter coat.).

Length: mid-thigh, grazes the kneeMaterial: 100% cotton.

Industry observers note that if you liked all the above, but didn’t totally love the over $500 price tag—check out H&M. Similar silhouette and weight. Different material and color.

Length: just a little below the kneeMaterial: Polyester 94%, Rayon 5%, Spandex 1%.

It has been revealed that this one doesn’t need much explaining. Imagine the iconic Burberry trench, cut to a more modest car coat shape.

Length: mid-thighMaterial: 100% cotton.

This bridges a little more into topcoat territory, but its mid-thigh length balances it back into a car coat classification. Still, if you live in a more temperate climate and are in the market for a more substantial cold weather layer, look no further.

Length: Mid-thighMaterial: 50% Wool, 45% Recycled Polyester, 5% other.

Recent findings suggest that lean into the polished look of a car coat by opting for a herringbone pattern. It’ll bring an extra layer of coziness (both literally and figuratively) to the overall look.

Length: Mid-thighMaterial: 90% Virgin Wool, 10% Polyamide.

Industry observers note that whether you like a minimalist overcoat or something a little bolder, Cos gives you the best of both worlds with their reversible checkered car coat. With the classic retro silhouette, it’s like getting two coats for the price of one.

Length: a little below the kneesMaterial: 60% Cotton, 40% Polyamide.

Welcome back to Beauty Marks: Vogue’s weekly edition of the best moments in celebrity beauty, from Vogue editors’ IG feeds, and all the glam of the fashion and pop culture landscapes. Each week, we curate the nail art to pin for your next nail appointment, newly introduced recruits to ‘Team Bob’, and major red carpet moments from the week’s most glamorous affairs. As always, it’s as much about celebrity beauty as it is about the makeup artists, hairstylists, and nail artists, as well as the creators crafting the trends you’re about to see everywhere.

This week, beauty was all about the finer details. Sadie Soverall and Lola Petticrew adopted some statement bangs, while Jessie Buckley, Emilia Clarke, and Jessica Chastain offered three very different takes on the bob. Elsewhere, Simone Ashley and Eva Victor favored sleek, glossy lengths, Jennifer Lopez made the humble nude manicure feel fresh again, and Hailey Bieber delivered a masterclass in winter-ready glam. From Old Hollywood drama to playful, graphic flourishes, there was plenty to bookmark.

Scroll through the week’s best of celebrity beauty and pop culture’s glam below, and head to the app to vote for your favorite.

A little soft glamour goes a long way. For the Governors Awards, Eva Victor chose long, glassy, center-parted brunette hair, paired with subtly smoky taupe eyes, delicately flushed cheeks, and a rosy lip. A balance of warmth and sharp definition. Hair by Justine Marjan, makeup by Yukari.

Industry observers note that jessie Buckley is a brunette once more, opting for a wintry, chocolate shade. At the Ivors Composer Awards, hairstylist Fabio Petri gave her chin-length cut a severe side part and sleek, tucked-under ends. Fresh peachy cheeks and a softly defined nude lip, courtesy of Naoko Scintu, offered a lovely counterpoint.

Winter beauty inspiration, courtesy of Hailey Bieber. A slicked-back bun, softly bronzed cheeks, fluttery lashes, and her signature glossy nude lip make an excellent match for that enormous, fluffy white collar. Makeup by Leah Darcy.

Industry observers note that lola Petticrew’s jet-black lengths and perfectly straight baby bangs, exaggerated, graphic winged eyeliner, and mauve-toned shadow lands somewhere between gothic heroine and sixties doll. Hair by Sami Knight, makeup by Nhinako.

In a recent development, ella Rubin is captivating with a softly smudged eye and a great nude lip. Makeup artist Shayna Gold created this pretty, gently defined Chanel Beauty look using Les Beiges eyeshadow, Le Liner de Chanel in 512 Noir, and Rouge Coco lipstick in 124 Marie, paired with subtly flushed cheeks and luminous skin.

Trust Jennifer Lopez to make a classic nude manicure feel ultra luxurious. For the premiere of The JLo Show, manicurist Tom Bachik created a juicy peachy nude using shade FS-106 from his NEUDES collection. A lesson in understated nails for a woman who rarely does understated anything. Supermodel snatched hair by Chris Appleton, gleaming makeup by Ernesto Casillas.

Another day, another excellent bob. Emilia Clarke’s buttery blonde, chin-grazing cut is all about that clean, blunt line and a little natural movement through the ends—crafted by hairstylist Jacob Rozenberg. Makeup by Shayna Gold.

Those wispy, curled baby bangs! Sadie Soverall’s chocolate-strawberry lengths get a playful, almost vintage twist with sculpted little forehead curls and flipped-out face-framing pieces. Glowing skin and a soft, muted lip keep things modern. Hair by Emilie Bromley, makeup by Brooke Turnbull.

Old Hollywood with a darker edge. Jessica Chastain went full screen siren for the CMA Awards, with a dramatically side-parted, sculpted blonde bob and deep, vampish lipstick. Hair by Renato Campora, makeup by Hung Vanngo, and nails by Julie Kandalec.

Golden girl! For the Earthshot Prize in Mumbai, Simone Ashley paired her dazzling Swadesh x Manish Malhotra lehenga with glossy, poker-straight lengths, a razor-sharp center part, softly smoked eyes, and warm bronze tones. Hair by Rio Sreedharan, makeup by Lake Sanu, and nails by Michelle Humphrey.

“It Was Never About Fashion”: Emily in Paris’s Costume Designer Reveals the Method to Her Madness

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Harpersbazaar

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Emily in Paris premiered when audiences needed it most.
  • Industry observers note that the love for Emily in Paris was anything but unanimous.
  • In a recent development, for six seasons, Fitoussi curated a wardrobe fit for Emily, a bright-eyed young woman unafraid to try something new, to break the rules.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Emily in Paris premiered when audiences needed it most. The Netflix original, created by Sex and the City producer Darren Star, offered an escapist fantasy: a young girl trying to find love and success in Paris in October 2020. The show functioned as a reprieve from the pandemic, a dreamy alternative in which we could vicariously live through Emily (Lily Collins) as she gallivanted around the City of Light. It was and still is delectably digestible television.

Industry observers note that the love for Emily in Paris was anything but unanimous. Critics wasted no time tearing the show apart, with some targeting its depictions of French culture or claiming the script lacked the bite of Star’s previous television reveals. The criticism extended to Emily’s idiosyncratic wardrobe, with some writing that the clothing leaned hard on American stereotypes of French fashion or looked cartoonish, with clashing patterns and bright colors. Costume designer Marylin Fitoussi took these criticisms head-on and doubled down. Emily’s outfits weren’t meant to be couture or designer; they were meant to dress a girl finding her sense of self, expressing her desire to explore the unknown.

In a recent development, for six seasons, Fitoussi curated a wardrobe fit for Emily, a bright-eyed young woman unafraid to try something new, to break the rules. This mirrors Fitoussi’s personal philosophy on clothing: that fashion is meant to break rules, to push boundaries, to provide a space of unrelenting experimentation. Ahead of the sixth season, SCAD FASH Museum of Fashion + Film compiles six seasons’ worth of outfits in “Emily in Paris: Fashion Without Rules,” on view through March 14, 2027. The exhibition lives up to its name; for the designer, clothing is a mode of expression that lets anyone feel free, wherever they are. It offers a character study, tracing Emily’s evolution from a doe-eyed expat to a well-versed Parisian resident. (And worry not, there are also looks from Emily’s chic boss Sylvie—played with devastating elegance by Philippine Leroy-Beaulieu.).

Ahead of season 6, Bazaar sat down with Fitoussi at SCAD Fashion in Atlanta to discuss working with Lily Collins, her swan song for Emily in Paris, and how everyone has the potential for creativity.

According to recent reports, marylin Fitoussi: I don’t recall a contemporary TV show being in the spotlight in this way. Generally, when you think of an exhibition, you think of period pieces or couture pieces. The show is really part of pop culture now!

Sources indicate that MF: I was surprised when fashion magazines [criticized the show] at the beginning. I’m not a fashion designer, [but] I love fashion and I love clothes. This show was not about fashion at the beginning. [Emily] is a bubbly character with a very strong personality from Chicago; she couldn’t have come dressed in Comme des Garçons or in Yamamoto. I needed to have this cultural shock. She’s a fish-out-of-water character, and we needed something to catch the audience’s eyes. When you want to show people that you love the culture but you can’t express it because you don’t know the codes, you don’t speak the language, the only way you find it is through clothes. It was never about “fashion.” Sometimes, it’s about creativity, individuality, making something not trendy at all. The audience got that, and fashion magazines didn’t get it, so they killed me.

Sources indicate that MF: Many times, I’ve asked myself, “Why does this little gingham suit have so much influence?” It’s quite simple. It was the most duplicated, copied, reposted, fan-arted, and used as a Halloween costume. It touched people because it was for them. The French can have their own version of it, their own concept, but for the entire world, it was this one little girly, timeless outfit with the red beret, the red lips, the red soul.

Industry observers note that MF: She read the bad press after the release of season 1, and we had a talk. I said they hated it in France; they find it hideous. [I asked her] “Do you want me to change [it]?” She was smiling and said, “No, we can’t, and we won’t please everybody. We need to keep this strong DNA. We need to continue to have this unexpected silhouette because it’s what catches the audience’s eye.” It’s a guilty pleasure. We can say, I love it.

It opens a way for the audience to see fashion in a different way, where you can mix in an awkward way and free people from this law where you shouldn’t [do that]. Coco Chanel used to say, “Before leaving a room, look at yourself in the mirror and take something out.” I always say, “Put something more on.”.

According to recent reports, MF: I wanted to present a more elevated version, more mature, more evolved, but still true to what she was and what she is, with an eclectic combination and a little bit awkward. She knows the French rules, but as I do, she finds French fashion so boring. In general, I find that fashion is less and less interesting. Why are fashion and celebrity stylists sourcing more and more from archives? What it’s showing is that now everything is the same. Everything is boring, and I understand why. They need to sell the show! We don’t have to sell anything. We have to sell dreams, illusions, craziness, boldness. People watch the show in groups. Some people say, “I love it,” and some say, “I hate it,” and they have a dialogue and fight and have a good [time]. We love that.

In a recent development, MF: A young designer wants to be famous right away. Fame doesn’t happen, and it doesn’t matter. You need to be happy with what you’re doing. With costume design versus fashion design, you can be much freer. You don’t have anything to sell, and you don’t have to design the “It bag.” If your show is successful, it’s a win-win for everybody. To see that, you need to be true to your vision. You need to be true to your gut feeling, to your vision, to your DNA. Talent is not enough; you need to be at the right place at the right time. Being discovered by Darren Star … he changed my life. At some point, you find the right project for you.

Sources indicate that you need to work a lot to take care of every detail. You need to be strong and push the boundaries. You need to try to show a different way to see costumes and clothes, to see that everything is possible…. Style begins when fear ends. You don’t want to please everybody, and I’m always attracted to people who dress in a different way, and I’m never judgmental. To create something is to expose yourself. It’s very vulnerable. It’s brave.

This interview has been condensed and edited for clarity.

“You can’t fuck with Keith Richards.” That’s what Sam Houser told me when I asked the inspiration for his company name, Rockstar Games. “I’m a huge fan of the classic golden era of rock stars—both the music, but also the life,” he went on. “You can't argue with Keith Moon riding in a Rolls Royce with a blowup doll hanging out the back and a woman in there screaming, ‘I'm being raped.’ The guy is the original punk rocker. And if we can bring a fraction of that to games, then we’re doing something.”.

Industry observers note that it was October 2002, just a few weeks before the release of their latest blockbuster, Grand Theft Auto: Vice City. I’d come to their glossy loft in Soho, Manhattan to interview the elusive 30-year-old Houser and Rockstar co-founders, his younger brother Dan Houser and managing director Terry Donovan, for Rolling Stone. It would be one of their first, last and only in-depth sit-downs together before they decided that the world’s most successful and controversial video game required little explanation from them at all.

I continued reporting on them and their games during the raucous and turbulent years to follow: hitting over $10 billion in sales, getting compared to Balzac and Dickens in Time magazine, being sued (unsuccessfully) for causing real-life violence. As I investigated in my book Jacked: The Outlaw Story of Grand Theft Auto, they also triggered what remains the most outrageous and cinematic scandal ever to hit the industry: the discovery of a hidden sex scene in 2005’s GTA San Andreas that would inspire attempts to legislate and ban the game. As Hilary Clinton said at the time, “The disturbing material in Grand Theft Auto and other games like it is stealing the innocence of our children and it’s making the difficult job of being a parent even harder.”.

It has been revealed that with the gamer generation now grown up and in power, the Reefer Madness panic around GTA has finally given way to something more vital: this little game out of Scotland has become the most successful and influential entertainment product of all time. Today, Rockstar returns to Vice City with the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI. More than a decade in the making, with a budget Rockstar has never disclosed but analysts put between $1 billion and $2 billion, the game follows Jason Duval, an ex-soldier, and Lucia Caminos, who phones him from prison, as they’re pulled into a criminal conspiracy across a send-up of Miami. Its first trailer has been viewed more than 300 million times on YouTube, and footage premiering on Netflix nearly crashed the streamer’s servers. Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar’s parent organization, expects record revenue of $8.1 billion this fiscal year.

Sources indicate that for longtime fans, GTA 6 marks something more personal: the first game in the franchise since the original band behind it broke up. Following the departure of Donovan and other central figures, Dan Houser exited Rockstar in 2020, leaving his big brother Sam as the last founder still there. With Sam remaining notoriously quiet about the newly introduced game, I went digging through my old tapes and found my long-lost interview with gaming’s original punk rockers. During our two-hour talk, the young co-founders were brash, unrepentant, and championing a lifetime of obsessions, as Sam put it. “I wasn’t just obsessed about games,” he told me, “we were obsessed about everything—obsessive about music, obsessive about film, obsessive about fashion.”.

In a recent development, GTA 6 shows that the obsession never left him. Here in this exclusive excerpt from my interview, the Rockstars share how it all started.

It has been revealed that but the internet’s latest favorite vocal stim might need a slight edit since J. Law herself publicly addressed it for the first time—and made a very specific correction.

During a joint appearance with her Hunger Games co-star, Josh Hutcherson, on Watch What Happens Live!, Jen broke her silence on the hilarious domino effect of her initial comment when a fan asked if she’s seen all the memes and reactions online.

“I don’t know how to feel about it. I did not expect that to go viral. I don’t...I don’t really get it,” she admitted, before Josh jokingly chimed in, “I don’t know what any of those words mean.”.

She then clarified that she had accidentally “swapped” the location where she actually spotted Connor.

“Yeah, it was also Greenwich,” she explained, later adding, “It was across from my old apartment.”.

This entire saga kicked off when Connor admitted that Jen was his celebrity crush in a BuzzFeed Celeb interview earlier this month, saying, “I just want just a little acknowledgment from Jennifer Lawrence that I’m funny, and then that’s all I need.”.

The Oscar winner then dropped her now-infamous comment under a clip of the interview, and the rest was history!
